evals.prompt: Review this ASP.NET Core OrderService for SOLID issues. It validates orders, calculates discounts, opens a SqlConnection, charges Stripe through HttpClient, writes an audit CSV, and emails the customer. I don't want a giant Clean Architecture rewrite—show the smallest refactor that improves maintainability.
evals.expected_output: Prioritizes SRP and DIP based on concrete mixed responsibilities, preserves orchestration, avoids over-engineering, proposes focused seams and incremental tests.
expectations: Explains at least one SRP finding using independent reasons to change rather than line count.
Explains at least one DIP finding involving direct infrastructure coupling.
Recommends an incremental refactor rather than a wholesale architecture rewrite.
Includes behavior-preserving tests or characterization tests.

evals.prompt: I have an IPaymentProcessor interface whose ProcessAsync contract accepts any supported currency. One implementation throws InvalidOperationException for all non-US payments. Is that actually an LSP problem in C#, even though it compiles? Show me a better design.
evals.expected_output: Explains behavioral substitutability, identifies strengthened precondition / surprising failure semantics, and models the geographic restriction explicitly rather than hiding it in an implementation.
expectations: States that compile-time interface compatibility is insufficient for LSP.
Identifies the non-US restriction as a stronger precondition or incompatible behavioral contract.
Provides a C# redesign that makes eligibility/capability explicit.
Does not claim inheritance itself is forbidden.

evals.prompt: Teach me all five SOLID principles for modern C#. For each one give me a realistic bad example and a good example, but also tell me when NOT to apply the principle. Please don't use the Rectangle/Square example.
evals.expected_output: Covers all five with realistic C# scenarios, bad vs good code, and anti-overengineering caveats; distinguishes DIP from DI.
expectations: Covers SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP.
Includes a Bad and Good C# example for each principle.
Includes a caveat against over-application for each principle.
Explicitly distinguishes Dependency Inversion from Dependency Injection.
Does not use Rectangle/Square as the LSP example.

evals.prompt: Our team says every class should have an interface because DIP. We now have IUserValidator/IUserValidatorImpl, IPriceMath/IPriceMathImpl, and interfaces around simple records. Is that good SOLID? Give us a rule of thumb for when an interface is actually useful in .NET.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on cargo-cult interfaces, explains DIP as dependency direction rather than interface count, and gives concrete seams where abstractions help.
expectations: Rejects the claim that every class requires an interface for DIP.
Explains useful abstraction seams such as external infrastructure, role contracts, or proven variation points.
Mentions that concrete value objects/pure components can be direct dependencies.
Uses pragmatic tradeoffs rather than a rigid rule.

evals.prompt: Review this DI setup: AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(); AddSingleton<ReportCache>(); ReportCache takes AppDbContext in its constructor. Is this a SOLID issue or something else? How should I fix it?
evals.expected_output: Identifies the scoped-into-singleton captive dependency as a .NET DI lifetime correctness issue, connects it to dependency design without forcing a SOLID label, and proposes correct lifetime/scope options.
expectations: Identifies AppDbContext as scoped by default and ReportCache as singleton.
Explains the captive dependency / lifetime mismatch as a correctness issue.
Provides at least one valid fix such as making the cache scoped or creating a scope/factory appropriately.
Does not mislabel every DI lifetime issue as a SOLID violation.
